title: Language Files
hints: Use clear, stable label identifiers and concise wording.

Reuse an existing label where the meaning is identical. Which trans-units exist is a property of the installation — every extension ships its own and an installation can override a language file through LANG/resourceOverrides — so search with typo3_label_lookup, which asks the installation, rather than working from memory.

hints.text: Reference a label by its translation domain (package.resource:key), not by the EXT: file path. The domain follows from the path and is registered nowhere: Resources/Private/Language/ is dropped, remaining directories become dot-separated snake_case parts, locallang.xlf becomes "messages", locallang_<suffix>.xlf becomes "<suffix>", any other file name becomes its own snake_case form, and Configuration/Sets/<Set>/labels.xlf becomes "sets.<set>".

Because the domain is derived rather than declared, a file a patch is about to add already has one. Call typo3_translation_domain_lookup with the path instead of guessing; a wrong guess only fails at runtime.

hints: Check whether language file normalization is needed.

title: Rendering and Registering Icons
hints: All of this is the backend's. The icon registry exists for modules, forms, lists and toolbars; a frontend template has no business in it and ships its own inline SVG or asset file. An identifier that looks like the shape a page needs is still a backend icon.

In Fluid: <core:icon identifier="actions-delete" size="small" /> with the core namespace, which is globally registered. Its arguments are identifier, size, state, overlay, alternativeMarkupIdentifier and title.

hints.text: In PHP: inject IconFactory and call $this->iconFactory->getIcon('actions-close', IconSize::SMALL)->render(). The size is the TYPO3\CMS\Core\Imaging\IconSize enum — cases DEFAULT, SMALL, MEDIUM, LARGE, MEGA and OVERLAY — which replaced the Icon::SIZE_* constants. getIconForRecord($table, $row) picks the identifier from the TCA schema.

hints: In TypeScript there are two entry points, and they are easy to confuse. For markup, the custom element <typo3-backend-icon identifier="actions-open" size="small"> from @typo3/backend/element/icon-element. For fetching an icon programmatically, the default export of @typo3/backend/icons, imported as Icons.

Identifiers follow <family>-<name> and spell the shape, not the intent: a warning is actions-exclamation-triangle, not actions-warning. Search the registry for the shape you want to see, not for the meaning you want to convey.

Which identifiers exist is a property of the installation, not of TYPO3: IconRegistry is assembled from every installed package. Validate one with typo3_icon_lookup, which reads all three sources of your installation — the T3Icons set, the Configuration/Icons.php of every package, and the flag images. An unknown identifier renders an empty box and fails at runtime, not at build time.

T3Icons come from the npm package and are not hand-added to a system extension. An icon that belongs to one extension is registered in its Configuration/Icons.php, which returns an array keyed by identifier with a provider (SvgIconProvider or BitmapIconProvider) and an EXT: source path.

title: How a Sitepackage Is Laid Out

hints.text: The core ships a theme of its own — the package typo3/theme-camino, typo3/sysext/theme_camino in a core checkout, absent from a Composer project that did not require it. It is where the layout below is worked out in full, so read it rather than invent one. Read, not depend on: it is the theme of one release line, announced to move out of the core into a repository of its own, and a project sitepackage that requires it or extends its set buys that migration for nothing.

hints: One template root carries all of it: Resources/Private/Templates/, with Pages/ for the page templates, Content/ for the content element templates, ContentPreviews/ for their backend previews, Layouts/, and Partials/ grouped in subdirectories. That directory is the single paths entry PAGEVIEW is given, and lib.contentElement is pointed at Templates/Content/ with the same Layouts/ and Partials/ — so the page and its content elements are rendered out of one tree instead of two.

A layout is addressed with its subdirectory: <f:layout name="Pages/Default" /> in a page template, <f:layout name="Content/Default" /> in a content element. The page frame and the content element frame are both called Default, and fluid_styled_content ships a Default of its own, so a shared Layouts/ root without those subdirectories renders the site header and footer inside every single content element — on a page that still comes back without an error.

One page layout per file in Configuration/BackendLayouts/<Name>.tsconfig, pulled in by the set's page.tsconfig with a single @import over that directory. The identifier the file declares below mod.web_layout.BackendLayouts is also what the page template is named after, so the file name, the identifier and Pages/<Name>.fluid.html are one name written in three places.

The template of a content element is derived from its CType rather than configured per element: lib.contentElement carries templateName.ifEmpty.cObject with case = uppercamelcase, so my_ext_text_teaser renders Content/MyExtTextTeaser.fluid.html. That is what makes a snake_case CType a requirement rather than a habit — words the identifier does not separate the file name does not separate either.

hints.text: The language files are split by who reads them — the frontend messages, the backend field labels, the backend layout titles, the content element previews. Each file is its own translation domain, and the domain is what a label is referenced by, so the split is what makes the references readable.

hints: page.<n> =< lib.fluidPage is a reference and not a copy: it is resolved while the page renders, out of the merged setup, so a data processor added to lib.fluidPage in a file that is imported later still arrives. The copy operator < is the one where the order of the imports decides what the object ends up holding.

title: Records in the Frontend Without Extbase

hints.text: A table of your own is a TCA file and nothing else: Configuration/TCA/<table>.php declares it and the schema is derived from those columns. Reading its records on a page needs no model, no repository and no controller — that is what a data processor is for, and Extbase enters the picture when pagination, search, validated arguments or forms do.

hints: The chain is configured as dataProcessing on the PAGEVIEW or on lib.contentElement: database-query with table, pidInList or uidInList and orderBy, and a nested dataProcessing of its own. record-transformation there turns the rows into record objects, files resolves the references of an image field, and comma-separated-value parses a text field that carries a table.

List and detail can be the same page. Fill the list variable unconditionally, fill the single record only when the request carries the argument — if.isTrue.data = GP:<argument> on that processor — and let the template branch on whether it is there. uidInList.data = GP:<argument> is safe on its own: the select is built by ContentObjectRenderer, which runs uidInList through GeneralUtility::intExplode() before it reaches the query.

hints.text: The site set ships the routing for it, in route-enhancers.yaml next to config.yaml. A detail view of that shape is a Simple enhancer whose routePath carries the argument, with a PersistedAliasMapper aspect naming the table and the slug field.

limitToPages takes an Expression Language string as well as a page uid, evaluated with page, site and siteLanguage — so an enhancer can be bound to every page of one backend layout instead of to a uid. That is what makes routing shippable at all: a set is installed into installations whose page ids nobody knows in advance, and of a site configuration shipped with an extension only rootPageId is remapped on import.

hints: The <title> of such a detail view is a PageTitleProvider and nothing else. RecordTitleProvider only reports a title that something else has set through setTitle(), and on a page that renders the record itself nothing does — so there is no TypoScript-only way to put a record's title into the head. The provider is a small class listed in config.pageTitleProviders, and it has to be public in Services.yaml.

title: Registering a Content Element

hints.text: A content element is a record type of tt_content, registered in Configuration/TCA/Overrides/tt_content.php with ExtensionManagementUtility::addRecordType(): the item — label, description, value, icon, group — then the showitem list for the type, then per-type overrides such as columnsOverrides, and optionally a position. The showitem list is the point: a type that does not bring one is a type whose backend form is somebody else's.

The predecessor is addPlugin() plus addToAllTCAtypes(), which registers the item and then patches the field list of every type. It is what an older extension looks like; a new record type is better added in one call.

addPlugin() is what is left for a plugin with a FlexForm, and it takes two arguments here — the item array and the FlexForm. The $field and $extensionKey arguments are gone, so the example that passes 'CType' and the extension key is from the branch before this one and is a TypeError on this one. It also seeds the new type's field list from the header type when the type declares none, so a plugin registered that way silently shows the header element's fields until a showitem replaces them.
A plugin is a CType like any other. The list_type detour, where one CType held every plugin and a second field chose between them, is gone, so what used to be a list_type value is a CType value now.

hints: ExtensionManagementUtility::addTcaSelectItemGroup() adds a group to the CType selector, positioned with before:<group> or after:<group>, so several elements of one extension arrive together instead of scattered through the list.

The backend preview of an element is a Fluid template registered in page TSconfig as mod.web_layout.tt_content.preview.<CType>, and the rendering definition is TypoScript: tt_content.<CType> on top of lib.contentElement. How the template name follows from the CType is in the sitepackage layout hint.

title: Documentation and Changelog
hints: User-facing behavior changes may need documentation or changelog entries.
A changelog file is needed for a Breaking change, a Deprecation, a Feature, or an Important message. A casual bug fix needs none — its commit message carries the information.

The filename is <Type>-<forgeIssueNumber>-<UpperCamelCaseDescription>.rst, in the directory of the minor version the change is released in; a backport goes into the <lts>.x directory of the oldest branch it reaches, in every branch that carries it.

The file opens with an include of /Includes.rst.txt, then an anchor of the form <type>-<issue>-<unique identifier> (a UNIX timestamp by convention), then the title "Type: #<issue> - <summary>" fenced by an overline and underline row of = at least as long as it, then "See :issue:`<issue>`".
Every type has a Description section; every type except Important has an Impact section; Deprecation and Breaking additionally have Affected installations and Migration.

The file ends with an .. index:: line carrying at least two and at most about five tags from the fixed list in typo3/sysext/core/Documentation/Changelog/Howto.rst. A Deprecation or Breaking file also carries exactly one of NotScanned, PartiallyScanned or FullyScanned.
A deprecation entry names the replacement and the migration path; without both it does not do its job. Add an extension scanner matcher when the deprecated API can be found statically.
Keep ReST changes focused and validate them before review.

title: Deprecated APIs
hints: Whether an API is deprecated is a property of the branch you work on, not of TYPO3 as a whole, and this server does not know your branch. Read the declaration itself: an @deprecated annotation together with a trigger_error(..., E_USER_DEPRECATED) call is what marks one.

What a branch deprecated is recorded in typo3/sysext/core/Documentation/Changelog/<version>/Deprecation-<issue>-<Title>.rst and in the matchers below typo3/sysext/install/Configuration/ExtensionScanner/Php/. Take the migration path from there instead of assuming a replacement.
A deprecated API keeps working until the next major release, so an existing call site is not automatically a defect. New code uses the replacement the changelog names.

Authoring a deprecation and finding out what a version deprecated are two directions through the same files. From the reading side: the changelog directory and the extension scanner matchers ship with the core and install packages of any installation, the Extension Scanner in the Install Tool runs the matchers over an extension, and `typo3 upgrade:list` and `typo3 upgrade:run` are the console side of the migrations.

title: Public Assets and the Publish Step
hints: Resources/Public/ of an installed package is published into the document root by the Composer installer, as a symlink below _assets/<hash>/. The hash is the package, not the file.

That publishing happens when the packages are installed, not at runtime. A file added to Resources/Public/ afterwards is not resolvable until they are installed again, and the remedy is a Composer install rather than a cache flush.

hints.text: The failure has a name: CanNotResolvePublicResourceException, thrown for a path that plainly exists on disk.
Nothing throws here — PathUtility computes the URL from the path either way — so the symptom is an asset that 404s in the browser rather than an exception in PHP.

hints: Reference such a file as EXT:<key>/Resources/Public/... and let the resolver produce the published URI. The _assets path is an implementation detail and its hash changes with the layout.

title: Upgrading an Installation
hints: The order is: find out what breaks, move the code, then the database, then the caches. Reading first is what makes it one pass instead of three — typo3_project_scope says which TYPO3 and PHP this installation is on and which extensions are its own, and typo3_changelog_lookup with type breaking or deprecation says what the target version did to them.

The third-party extensions decide when the upgrade can happen, not whether it should. One without a release for the target major blocks the whole step, and Composer's own resolution is where that surfaces — so require the new constraints for typo3/cms-* and for every extension in one call rather than one at a time, and read the conflict it reports as the list of what has to be replaced, patched or dropped.

Raise the PHP version the target requires before the TYPO3 constraint, in composer.json and in the environment that actually runs it — a DDEV project states its own in .ddev/config.yaml. Resolving against a PHP nobody runs produces a lock file that installs and an installation that does not boot.

Everything up to here is revertible with git and everything after it is not. Take a database dump before the first command that writes, and do the pass on a copy: the schema changes and the upgrade wizards are what makes an upgrade one-way.

After the packages changed, `typo3 extension:setup` is the step that applies them: database schema changes, static data, the setup of every installed extension. It is the core's own command — `database:updateschema` belongs to the TYPO3 Console extension (helhum/typo3-console), which an installation only has if it required it.

Then the wizards. `typo3 upgrade:list` shows what is pending and why, `typo3 upgrade:run` runs all of them and takes a single wizard identifier as an argument. A wizard states its own prerequisites — a schema that is up to date, a current reference index — so one that refuses usually means a step above was skipped.

hints.text: `typo3 upgrade:mark:undone <identifier>` marks a wizard as not run, which is the way back from one that ran against the wrong data. Without it a wizard is done for good.

hints: Then `typo3 cache:flush`, and `typo3 cache:warmup` where the first request must not pay for the rebuild.

What no wizard touches is your own code. The Extension Scanner in the Install Tool runs the core's matchers from typo3/sysext/install/Configuration/ExtensionScanner/Php/ over an extension and finds the call sites a changelog entry named. How much of a change it can find at all is what that entry's FullyScanned, PartiallyScanned or NotScanned tag says, and typo3_changelog_lookup returns it.

Run the sequence in the environment that is safe to break first, then the same commands in the same order everywhere else. An upgrade that was done differently on production is an installation nobody can reproduce — and the site configuration, the TypoScript and the TSconfig are part of what has to be re-checked there, not only the PHP.
